title: Rank a list without sorting it

screens.prompt: Put Ada's place in the team into C2 using the default order, without sorting the sheet.

hints.syntax: RANK takes the value, then the whole column: =RANK(B2,B2:B6).
hints.func-rank: Counting the numbers larger than 58 gives the place by hand. RANK does that count against the range.
hints.require-ref: The second argument is the range B2:B6, so every swimmer is in the comparison.
hints.value: With no order argument the largest time takes place 1, so Ben's 61 is first and Ada's 58 is second.
hints.error: #N/A means the value is missing from the column being ranked, often because the two arguments point at different rows.

reject.why: right arithmetic, wrong tool — the sheet should say rank, not count-if-plus-one
the third argument reverses the order, so Ada is ranked fourth-slowest instead
Ben's place, 1, sitting in Ada's row
the range excludes B2, so the fast times are outside the ranking
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma means the arguments never separate

screens.prompt: Flip the order argument so the smallest time takes place 1, and put Ada's place in C2.

hints.syntax: The third argument sets the order, and 1 counts up from the smallest: =RANK(B2,B2:B6,1).
hints.func-rank: This is the same ranking read from the other end, and RANK takes the order as its third argument.
hints.require-ref: Point the second argument at B2:B6 instead of typing the five times.
hints.value: Counting up, Eli's 50 is place 1, then 55 and 57, so Ada's 58 is place 4.
hints.error: A text value in the first argument gives #VALUE!, because RANK cannot put a word in order.

reject.why: the descending place, 2, not the ascending one
Ben's ascending place, 5, in Ada's row
the range leaves out B2, so two swimmers are missing from the comparison
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing commas jam three arguments into one
the second smallest time, 55, which is a value rather than a place
twice the ascending place, 8, which is not a place at all

docs.explain:
RANK compares one value against a range and returns the place it takes. The optional third argument sets the direction: 0 or nothing ranks the largest number first, and any other value ranks the smallest first. The range needs anchoring with dollar signs so it does not slide when the formula is filled down.

On this sheet the times run 58 in B2, 61 in B3, 55 in B4, 57 in B5 and 50 in B6. Ranked from the largest down, 61 takes place 1 and Ada's 58 takes place 2. A third argument of 1 turns the order round, and her 58 becomes place 4 with Eli's 50 at the top.

Equal values share a place and the next one is skipped, so two swimmers on 61 are both first and nobody is second. A total built by adding ranks will then miss a number, because a rank names a row and does not count rows.

errors.text: The value being ranked is not in the range, which happens when the number argument points at a different row from the list.
The number argument is text, so there is nothing to compare with the other values.
A third argument of 1 ranks the smallest value first, so a missing argument flips every place on the sheet.

docs.atWork: A league table showing each swimmer's place on the row they already sit in, and the same sheet ranked the other way for handicaps.
docs.outcome: Put a place number on every row of an unsorted list, in either direction.
docs.teaches: RANK, and anchoring the range it compares against
docs.dataset: A team of swim times ranked both ways

seo.title: RANK in Excel: place a list without sorting
seo.description: RANK compares each row against one anchored range. Leave the range unanchored and it slides as you fill down, so every row ranks against a different slice.
